If we granted war veterans' allowance to men who served in South Africa, it might be quite difficult to refuse, as we do under the legislation, to grant war veterans' allowance to those who served only in Canada or in England during the last war. It opens a wide field and I suggest to my right hon. friend that if he will think the matter over- I shall do the same myself-we may be able next year to bring down some recommendation to parliament with respect to this matter. I can only say that last year during the sittings of the parliamentary committee the question was considered and the committee did not deem it advisable to make a special recommendation to have the South African war veterans placed on war veterans' allowance.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
With a great deal of what the minister has said I am wholly in accord. I realize the difficulty of establishing with respect to pensions a principle that cannot be supported on any broad grounds, but it is because of that very fact that I venture to put before the committee the suggestion I have offered, not that I am doing it for the first time, for the suggestion has been put before the minister by others. The truth is that a substantial fund with which we began at the time of the war became merged into the larger fund and was utilized for the common benefit of all-that is, including those of the great war and those who fought in South Africa. It is quite true that at this time of day to speak of the privations and sufferings of the men who were in South Africa, suggesting that they are in a burnt-out condition in 1937, would be rather to impose upon the credulity of those upon whom you press that argument. Realizing that, I was trying to see whether the claim could not be put on the other ground. For it is quite clear that if the fund had not been exhausted they would still be receiving-I am speaking of the extreme cases-some support from that fund. From time to time we did take care of outstanding cases, and it was with regret that we found the fund entirely depleted; it was because of the great claims upon it during the later years subsequent to the war that it was so rapidly depleted. It must be remembered, however, that the "burnt-out" allowance provided for by statute has taken the place of any claims which might be preferred against that fund. That is beyond question. I realize that the matter cannot be dealt with merely by the minister's saying so; it must be covered by statute. All I wish to do is to suggest that it is worthy of the most careful consideration in the light of the
circumstances to which I have alluded. But I should like also to point out that there must be some error in the computation. There were 5,200 men who went to South Africa and subsequently 2,000 who turned round and came back. I believe they landed only for exercise and did not take part in hostilities. That left, therefore, 5,200, and it must be an error to say that 5,000 survive.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I am beginning to think that. I shall be only too glad to check and give the figures.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: And the suggestion that 5,000 or 5,200 survived is, of course, entirely astray.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: No, 7,000 all told.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: But 2,000 did not figure in the matter at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: In proportion there would be something like 3,000 surviving.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I think that is what must be meant. One speaks with great reserve, but I think that is too large a number, because it must not be forgotten that a substantial number of those who served in South Africa volunteered their services in the great war, and in the early stages there were great losses of that type of experienced soldier. In addition, a number have departed this life because they were of an age subject to mortality at a higher rate than would otherwise be expected. The guess that there are 843 survivors who would be in a position to make claims, could, I believe, be subject to a very exact check. My information, whatever it may be worth- and one must always remember that there is no accurate information available-is that something less than 500 are, under any circumstances, liable to make claims, and one could reduce that again to something less than 300 as the number throughout Canada who would be likely to do so. I think in the interim the minister might have a close study made, and while this would involve some time, the records are such that it is possible to do it. Those who, it is asserted, are not otherwise engaged might find in this ample scope for their activities during their very desirable leisure. Perhaps that would meet the situation as sometimes expressed by hon. members on the other side of the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I shall be very glad to have an inquiry made.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
In this connection I avail myself of the precedent which the right hon. leader of the opposition is trying to establish to go a little further into the past and ask for something for those who took part in the repression of the Northwest Rebellion in 1885.
1314	COMMONS
Supply-Pensions-European War

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: They are looked after.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Well, I have a case of one of my oldest electors, Medard Boulais, who is, I think, now eighty-six years of age. He was under General Laurie in the Northwest Rebellion. He used to be sent ahead of the army as a scout; he did that very dangerous duty for the whole period of the rebellion. He was also the scout for the Queen's Own of Toronto, and as a consequence of his service in 1885 he lost his right to his homestead. In those days these regiments used to take horses, and General Laurie asked him to take with him a team of horses for that purpose. He lost his horses and he lost his homestead. After the rebellion he decided to go to the Yukon where he engaged in prospecting. He is now sick and he has no means whatsoever. He is starving, if I may use the word, because he has to rely upon the charity of friends. I think the Department of Pensions and National Health should do something for a case like that. Mr. Boulais wrote to the department and was told that he had no right to a pension. The last letter he wrote to the department was on December 12, 1936, and on January 27, 1937, he received from the president of the pension bureau a letter stating that his request had been studied and the department regrets to inform him that there is no statute or bylaw by virtue of which he can obtain a pension for his services in that rebellion. If there is no statutory provision for pensions for Northwest Rebellion veterans, there must be something to allow this department to save this man from starving. He is eighty-five years of age and very sick. I have put the matter before the minister in the hope that he will find a way to do something for this citizen.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Pensions for Northwest Rebellion veterans are awarded on recommendation by the Department of National Defence, but to establish his right to pension a man must show that he was disabled during the rebellion. The matter to which reference was made in the discussion between the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) and myself dealt with the statute which provides for war veterans' allowance, that is to men who are burnt out. It provides that such burnt-out men, whose disability is presumed to be due to service, shall obtain S20 per month if unmarried and $40 if married, if they are permanently incapacitated from carrying on their occupation or if they have reached the age of sixty.
In the case cited by my hon. friend the same result could easily be obtained if the man in question would apply for old age pension in Quebec. He would receive $20 per month under that.
fMr. Dupuis.]

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: And in the one case he is eligible and in the other he is not.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I should like to add my voice to that of the leader of the opposition in regard to the plight of South African veterans. I appreciate very much the fact that the minister is interested and is going to give their problem serious consideration.
I have had numerous letters from men who served in the South African war, and I know their plight is sad indeed. I would ask the minister to give this problem as early consideration as possible, because as far as. I can find out the majority of these men are from sixty-five to sixty-eight years old and so are not eligible for an old age pension.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: My difficulty is to find a broad principle which will permit the South African war veterans to come in under this act, and at the same time keep in force the restrictive provisions of the War Veterans' Allowance Act as now existing. It was instituted on the presumption that men who served overseas in the last war were in some cases prematurely aged, and if I can possibly find any such principle as that to apply to South African war veterans I shall be only too glad.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: In fairness to the South African war veterans it should be pointed out that the principle is not quite as clear as the minister suggests. The War Veterans' Allowance Act I understand applies to all men who served in France or other theatre of war. There are thousands of Canadian soldiers who were in France but were not in the front lines, and possibly not under as heavy shell fire as those in South Africa. Then there are Canadians who served in Great Britain, or only in Canada, who are eligible under the War Veterans' Allowance Act provided they are small pensioners. On the other hand the South African veterans were subject to disease to a far greater extent than were the Canadian troops in France.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: There was no inoculation for typhoid then,

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Probably they had to undergo sufferings at least as great as those of a proportion of the Canadians who were in France. I do not think the principle is quite as clear-cut as the minister says, so I would add my word to that of my leader in asking that the question be given further consideration.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Far be it from me to compare the sufferings of those who served in the South African war with

Supply-Pensions-European War
the sufferings of those who suffered .in the recent great war. I am sure, however, that those who served in South Africa suffered much more from the effects of heat than did the soldiers in France. I am sure also that the former did not get as good food supplies that we received, nor could they possibly get as good water supplies that we obtained. Further, as has been pointed out, there was no inoculation for typhoid at that time, and I believe typhoid was rampant among the soldiers in the South African war while there was scarcely a case of it among those who served in the last war. Also, as has been said by the right hon. leader of the opposition, most of those who served in the South African war also enlisted in the last war. They had a great sense of loyalty, and I would think a very large percentage of those veterans enlisted under the colours as soon as the last war broke out. I certainly believe they should receive every consideration from this government.
But, Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that another class which should also receive consideration is composed! of those who did not serve in France but who left Canada and got only as far as England. A great many of these men are not receiving a five per cent pension. The difference between a man who cannot get a five per cent pension and a man who does get it is very small, because a five per cent pension means a very minor ' disability indeed. But if a man receives a five per cent pension even though he served only in England, he is entitled! to the war veterans' allowance. My point is that the man who does not happen to get a five per cent pension is in most cases, just as much entitled to the war veterans' allowance as the man who gets a pension of that percentage. When a man enlisted he had to give up his former m,ode of living. Many of those who got only to England had to devote long hours to the service of their country. They worked in offices and did other kindls of work to which they were not accustomed, but because they have no disability they are not entitled to the allowance.
While we are on this question I think something should be said about the widows of those veterans who, at the time of their death were receiving the war veterans' allowance. As I understand the law, at the present time the veteran who is entitled to this allowance gets $40 a month if he is married, but on his death the widow is notified that she will continue to get the allowance for one year only. If the man became pre-aged and incapable of working because he served in the war, surely when he dies his widow should not be cut off entirely. When this survey is being
made in order to determine how many South African veterans are entitled to this allowance, I would ask the minister that it be extended to include also those who left the shores of Canada and served in England, who may claim this allowance. I would ask also that great consideration should be given to the claims of these widows. I do not suggest that they should receive $40, but I think the widow should receive a small amount of money not , only for one year after her husband's death but during her lifetime. I would ask the minister to give that point very careful consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I shall be very glad to do so.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Among others, two points have been raised by the hon. member, the first of which deals with the preference given under the Civil Service Act to ex-soldiers. Speaking offhand, but I think fairly accurately, I believe I may have to correct the hon. member in some of his statements with respect to preference given to pensioners over non-pensioners who served overseas.
1316	COMMONS
Supply-Pensions-European War
The preference to pensioners is a peculiar one, and is given them provided they have not as yet successfully reestablished themselves. There are one or two other conditions, but the important point is that if after his return from overseas a pensioner has been successfully reestablished, he does not enjoy the preference. I believe I could give an instance which may make the matter more clear. We will take the case of a man who, prior to his service in the war, was a railway conductor but who, when he returned from overseas, was able to follow his former occupation on the railway, and did so for a period of five or six years. It does not matter what period of time he serves, he is considered to have been successfully reestablished, and even though he be a pensioner the civil service commission will not give him a preference over the ex-soldier who is not in the enjoyment of a pension, but has seen service overseas.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: He still has the exsoldier's preference.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
But not the pensioner's
preference. Then, there are a number of other cases. Only recently there was an endeavour in my department to establish preference in a case something like this: The civil service commission called for applications for the position of nurse at one of the hospitals. A person who immediately after leaving the army had got married and had no experience in nursing for twenty years following the war endeavoured to set up a preference for herself on the ground that she had had service overseas and had not been successfully reestablished. I am not quite sure yet as to whether I shall not be obliged to reject this person's application, if she comes at the head of the list, on the obvious ground that not having been in nursing service or training for the profession of nursing for that period of time she would not be as competent to look after the rapidly aging ex-soldiers in our hospitals as would some other person who had been training or acting as a nurse in the past twenty years. I believe the illustration will cover one of the points brought up by the hon. member, namely preference within the preference accorded the pensioner.
The hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Elliott) was about to discuss the second matter on Tuesday last, namely as to whether or not those who obtained pensions should be permitted to continue in the enjoyment of it and at the same time draw reasonably high salaries in the civil service. Concerning this point I have had a memorandum prepared. I 
do not wish to tire the committee by reading all of it, but the matter contained therein goes back to 1916. In a special committee formed in 1916, of which I believe the only member now present is the right hon. the leader of the opposition, a recommendation was made:
That, to encourage industry and adaptability, no deduction be made from the amount awarded to such pensioner owing to his having undertaken work or perfected himself in some form of industry. The welfare of the state demands that so far as possible those who are at all able should endeavour to augment their pension allowance. If the pension granted were subject to reduction owing to the recipient having remunerative work, your committee are of the opinion that a premium would be put on shiftlessness and indifference.
The principle seemed to have been accepted by the house, without very much discussion, with the exception that Mr. W. F. Nickle, K.C., of Kingston, one of those who in 1919 framed the first pension legislation, said this:
The committee took perhaps a radical step in another matter, but a step that seems to me to have been fair. They said that a man in receipt of a pension should be entitled to the fruits of his labour, that if a man who had lost his eyes adapted himself to circumstances and was able to earn the means of life, if he had lost his feet or his hands and had the pluck to again face life and through the advantage of vocational training or otherwise was able to secure employment in another sphere of activity, that man was entitled to keep what he earned. The committee took the stand that if those who had suffered greatly in this war had the courage when they returned to endeavour to earn a fresh place for themselves in civil life, they' should be paid their pension in respect of the physical disability they had suffered, and should also be entitled to what earnings they made, and that the earnings should not be deducted from the pension.
To adopt any other scheme than this seemed to the committee to have as an inevitable result the encouragement of shiftlessness and laziness and the committee felt that in a country like this everything possible should be done to encourage the men to take on themselves fresh employment when they again returned to this country.
The same principle was carried on, all through the recommendations of the various parliamentary committees, down to to-day. I need not quote the findings of other committees. The Ralston commission, which thoroughly investigated every phase of soldier problems, reported in a similar manner.
In 1933 it was thought there was some intention on the part of the then Minister of Finance, the Hon. Mr. Rhodes, to change the principle or in some way take away from those who were in receipt of pension either such pension or some of the salary attached to the positions they held in the civil service.

Supply-Pensions-European War

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: But he modified that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Yes, I am coming to that. On reconsideration the Hon. Mr. Rhodes said:
The last thing in the world that we had in mind was any interference with the sanctity of a contract concerning pensions. Whatever merit there may be or may not be attached to the suggestions contained in the budget speech with respect to pensions, it was never intended to interfere with pensions as such.
The point is that when the men came back from overseas they were told, "You will receive pensions, but go ahead and get jobs wherever you can. Not only that, but we will give you preference in the civil service of Canada in order to permit you to augment your pension by working for the government." I submit it would be something almost equivalent to a breach of faith if at this late date, after a great many of them have successfully reestablished themselves and have succeeded in filling some of the highest positions in the civil service, and despite their physical handicaps have been able to overcome them and render good service to the state, we were to deprive them of their pensions or to decrease their salaries. More-ever, an example such as that to private firms or organizations would not be in the best interests of the state or of industry.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I was anxious to obtain from the minister a statement concerning those against whom there has been discrimination. They do not want others to lose their pensions. However, they are told, when seeking a civil service position, that if they had pensions it would be easier for them to obtain that position. They are met with the statement, "although you have no pension, those who have are in a preferred position, when they apply for this work." There are a great many ex-soldiers living in my riding and many of them have become distinguished citizens. They did their share in the last war and are proud of having done it, but a certain number of them are handicapped in the way I mentioned. I think it is my duty to bring this matter before the minister.
By the way, I was invited to some of their meetings and they unanimously passed a resolution approving the government's policy of national defence. Many of them told me that while they hoped there would never be another war like the one in which they took part, they would still be ready to do their part should the need arise. It is for such citizens as these that something should be done to help them, not to receive pensions, because they were not wounded, but to obtain the work they want. It may be said that civilians are discriminated against in favour
of ex-soldiers, but I think any reasonable citizen will agree that that is only right. The only point I want to make is that the returned soldier without a pension should be on the same level as the returned soldier who receives compensation for his services in the war.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: When a man receives $6,000, $8,000 or $10,000 as salary, would his pension be discontinued? Is there a certain peak in earning when that action is taken?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: That is not taken into consideration in any way. As I have indicated, the pension is based upon war services and has nothing whatever to do with civilian occupation.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the minister referred to the report of the committee which sat during the recess in 1916 and 1917. Ever since we established pensions in this country we have kept two principles in mind. The first one is that the pension is in no sense wages or salary; it is compensation, inadequate in many cases, for injuries suffered by the recipient. The second principle is that in the computation of salary or wages which a man might receive, it is to be taken that that is based upon the service he renders and the service he renders can have no relation to the pension he receives for the injuries he suffered during the war.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: May I interrupt my right hon. friend to call to his attention another principle. The scale of pension is based upon a man's capacity to earn in the common labour market and has no relation to the occupation which he followed prior to the war.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
As the minister suggests, the pension which a man receives is in no sense predicated upon what he was receiving, but is based upon his then value in the labour market. The hon. gentleman wants to know what would be done in the case of a man receiving $8,000 or $10,000 as salary and being paid a pension of, let us say, $500. I remember having to meet that argument and I found it difficult to do so until I thought the matter out. The answer is that the services which the man is able to render in his then condition are worth $8,000 a year and presumably he would get that, if he renders the services adequately and efficiently, whether or not he had ever been to war. The fact that he went to war and suffered injuries which entitles him to $500 has no relation to the salary which he receives for the services he now renders, whether they be to the state or to someone else. That matter was discussed

Supply-Pensions-European War
by the committee in 1916. I sometimes regret that I was not a candidate in 1917 so that I could have followed up some of the work done by that committee during the recess.
There is another matter upon which the private member who is now Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Power) had very strong views. This matter was raised this afternoon by the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville (Mr. Dupuis). There is a question whether the preference given to returned men might not be open to criticism in 1937. Conditions are to some extent different to-day from what they were in 1919 or 1920. A new generation of younger men has arisen and we now have the possibility of older men being given preference, say for a post office job, when a younger man might be more suitable for the position. I believe I am right in stating that no consideration is given to the matter of age.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Quite right.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
The question arises as
to whether or not that greater preference is fair to the public service. At this time I think much may be said in this regard. However, the statute is there and notwithstanding the views that may be taken with respect to the desirability of it when one is not in office, it is an entirely different matter to say whether or not one is prepared to suggest this repeal when one is responsible. May I say to my hon. friend, the member for Chambly-Rouville, that the act will likely remain. It will terminate its usefulness only by what is euphemistically spoken of as the effluxion of time. I notice in the report which the minister handed me a moment ago that there are only forty pensioners left from the South African war. These pensions were paid originally by the British government.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: There are forty disabilities and three dependants.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
That indicates that the
number we were mentioning, 863, is probably an over statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: There were only 219 deaths among Canadians who served in the South African war.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
The hon. member for
York West (Mr. Streight) was one of those who early went to South Africa, and during the last war he took with him quite a number of those who were in South Africa. Perhaps he would give the committee the benefit of his knowledge, which he has just communicated to me, and which I am sure will be helpful in the future with respect to the

matter we have just discussed. The pensions paid to the men who went to the South African war were paid by the imperial government. In 1920, after the great war, we raised the pensions being paid to these men to what they would have received had they served in the great war. It seems to me that this fact offers an additional reason for looking into the matter from the angle I suggest.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I would ask the minister where he got his information regarding the hardships of the South African campaign as compared with the hardships in the late war. I also think his figure of 7,000 troops who went to South Africa from Canada, if he took the trouble to look it up, would be raised to about 10,000, and I think his figure of about 5,800 South African veterans being alive to-day would be reduced perhaps 3,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I believe that is correct, but I shall have the exact figures to-night.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I would be surprised if there are 3,000 South African veterans alive in Canada to-day. Speaking of pensions for these veterans, it is quite true that the South African campaign was not comparable with the late war so far as slaughter was concerned. Nevertheless, the South African veterans did go through hardships and trials that we did not experience in the late war. For instance, in South Africa we had to contend with bad water, poor food, and severe climatic conditions. We had not only the heat but the cold. Anyone who knows what the South African climate is like, knows the nights are very cold, and the veterans had to sleep on the cold veldt sometimes with one blanket, and sometimes with a couple of inches of snow around them. I feel that any veteran who has served in any campaign-go back to the rebellion of 1885, or even back to the veterans of 1866-should come under the same heading as the South African veterans. I do not see why they should be discriminated against in any shape or form. Take the South African veterans at the beginning of the great war. Who formed the framework of every battalion in the first division? It was the South African veterans. They were at a premium. They were made sergeants and officers. I was one myself; I know. The framework of our first contingents and of some of the later ones was made up of those who had seen service in South Africa. I hope the minister will not forget to remember these veterans who served in Africa, and if he will look into the matter he will find that a great number of these veterans gave their lives in the great war. I had in my own

Supply-Pensions-European War
unit twenty who had served in South Africa, and they never came back from the great war. It was stated a few moments ago that the average age at present of the South African veteran was sixty-six or sixty-seven. I am only fifty-six myself.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Did the hon. member run away from school?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Just about. I know there are in Canada a number around my own age who served in South Africa. I think not only the veterans of 1885 but even the 1866 veterans should be given a fair show with those who served in the late war.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I want to add a word in support of what was said by the hon. member for Brantford City (Mr. Macdonald). There have come to my attention quite recently a number of sad cases of widows of pensioners, and1 I have referred to the war veterans' bureau two or three very distressing cases. These widows have reached the age of fifty to sixty. Probably during the lifetime of the pensioner the nominal pension that was allotted was received. Then the husband died. There was possibly a small mortgage on the home. In these cases the widow is in ill health; she is not able to carry on and the property has been lost. It is a very distressing outlook for the widow, whose husband served and gave of his best, to be faced with a situation like that, and I do want to support and urge upon the minister what the hon. member for Brantford City has said in that connection.
The other matter I would mention was raised by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green). The minister intimated that there were certain hospitals other than military ones, being contacted by the department in connection with hospitalization. May I ask if that is correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Yes, civilian hospitals under contract with the department.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: How many of those hospitals are there?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Nearly four hundred throughout Canada.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
It would seem evident to any member of the committee that if a soldier was fit at the time of his enlistment and was unfit at the time of his discharge, he became unfit during his service; but in numerous cases, although, according to the medical report, soldiers have been wounded or suffering from some illness during their service, on discharge they are considered as fit by the board and the appeal court.
At this point may I bring to the attention of the committee a very serious case. It is of one of the doctors of the pension department whose name I do not recall, who went to the war and had two or three years at the front or in the army counted as years in university. Afterwards some imagination was used in his case and he was received as a doctor without having the necessary knowledge. His experience in the hospital was very short; he is only a clerk, just the same as a municipal clerk or a man who writes or examines forms, but he is one of the examiners of the department. I do not care whether he is Liberal or Conservative; that does not interest me, but it does seem that doctors in charge of the examination of soldiers who ask for pensions should be well qualified. War service does not count in such qualification; it is the medical experience that matters. I draw the attention of the minister to that case, which he knows very well, in order that there may be some redress. At the present time, if a soldier suffers from some internal sickness like rheumatism contracted at the front, as may well be seen from his medical sheet, he does not receive much consideration from the board or from the appeal court. General Turner-I have forgotten his initials, I think it is R. W.-may be a great soldier but he is no doctor and his decisions are very poor ones. I say that with personal knowledge of the cases. I know soldiers who at times are hardly able to walk on account of their disability. I have in mind one case, regimental number 897, one of the first men to enlist, who has been most unfairly treated by the appeal board. I denounce the appeal board on account of that. We do not need a brilliant soldier; we need a good sound doctor on the appeal board. It is not a matter of considering the war record of any soldier; it is a matter of seeing whether this poor soldier has suffered any disability from the time he enlisted until the time of his discharge. That seems very simple and clear, but it is hard to make those people understand it. And it is the same thing with the other fellow who signs most of the reports. We have enough of that. It seems to me that
a poor fellow who is anxious to receive fair treatment should have it not only from a good fellow but from a competent medical man. Therefore I ask the minister if he would kindly do a little spring-cleaning in his department. There is bureaucracy of every kind in every department. I do not blame the minister for that, but there is the curse of bureaucracy in the Department of Pensions as well as in others. Once I recommended a soldier for treatment at Ste. Anne de Bellevue hospital. He went there and they extracted all his teeth and sent him home. They said, You are all right; go home. I had to apply to Doctor MacLaren, who is now Lieutenant Governor of New Brunswick, in order that this man should be supplied with false teeth by a dentist in Riviere du Loup. This is not the treatment that should be given to a man who has risked his life for his country. The man had a very good record. For all these considerations I ask the minister to use his broom in his department and see that the cobwebs are swept away.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I should like to support the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) in his plea for more consideration to some of the returned men who suffer from disease. I believe there are men whose records do not show very much or any disability during service, but who subsequently developed something that cost them a great deal of inconvenience or suffering for the balance of their lives. At the moment I have in mind the case of a young man named McEleese who served the guns in France for more than three years and who, in May, 1919, took his discharge, apparently quite well. Then, in November, 1919, he fell iff, and he has been paralysed ever since. The original diagnosis was sleeping sickness. This man is living in Regina. There is nothing on his sheet that would indicate any cause for his condition such as we sometimes find on soldiers' sheets, but it is believed that the condition from which this man is suffering is due in no small measure to nerve shock which he sustained during the war in the capacity in which he served. For a long time he was in Regina, cared for by friends, and then was transferred to an old folks' home. To-day he is back in the city which is maintaining him as an indigent, as it does for aged persons without means, paying I think it is a dollar a day for maintenance in a private home in that city.
Here we have a young man who has been paralysed for the last sixteen or seventeen years and who, during all that time, has been endeavouring to have his case reviewed. I
1322	COMMONS
Supply-Pensions and National Health
am hoping that the commission will consider such cases sympathetically. I believe they will. I may say I took up this matter with the minister some months ago and he referred me to the commission, but up to the present time I am afraid nothing has been done. That is a type case, and I take it that there are many other cases of that kind. I have been informed also that sleeping sickness is now believed to be of long incubation. I know very little about that phase of the matter, but that is what I am told, and if that is so it is entirely possible that the germ was present when this man was discharged in May, 1919. I am asking the department to look into cases such as these, and I am sure members of this house would be only too glad to see something done for men who served but who to-day are bedridden and. without assistance because of a former or improper diagnosis.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Before this item is passed, Mr. Chairman, I should like to remind you that some time ago I endeavoured to ask a question of the minister. We have a quorum that visits the different provinces. In some cases a man is granted a five per cent disability and is recommended for pension, but when his papers come to Ottawa, for some reason or another the pension board here refuses to pay that five per cent. Then the matter is referred to a quorum or to the appeal board, and I have had two or three cases where the award which was recommended by the quorum was not paid. Even if it is a small amount, only five per cent, it would be of great assistance to him, because once a man is in receipt of a pension, though it be ever so small, there are other benefits which accrue to him. He can get free transportation to Camp Hill hospital; he can get assistance from the board during the winter months. So if he is refused this small pension, a real injustice is done.
I have voiced my disapproval of the appeal board refusing pensions such as these after the quorum has recommended that they be paid. The quorum is right on the spot; it examines the man and takes the evidence of the doctor who treated him, and if the quorum is satisfied that it is a genuine case surely the pension should not be refused here in Ottawa. It does not seem to me that these men are fairly dealt with.
A little later I should like an explanation from the minister, if possible, of a case which I have in my own home town. I doubt whether there is another case in Canadla; at the most there must be very few. This man enlisted in Newfoundland, with a Newfoundland regiment. He went overseas with that regiment and, being a seafaring man, when he

*was over there he requested permission to leave the regiment and join up with the navy. Permission was granted1; he joined the navy and served during the whole war with great distinction. He won recognition for prize money, and he was awarded different medals. All in all he had a distinguished career. After the close of the war he came back and was demobilized1 in Canada. To-day that man is a complete cripple. I have taken up his case with the government of Newfoundland and with the British government. I have taken it up also with the Canadian Department of Pensions, but while this man gave such splendid service to the British Empire, not one of these three countries he served is willing today to own him in any shape or form. They say, "No, he is not our care, but we will try in every way to get consideration for him." He has been refused a pension time and time again. His application was refused for so long, and he had such a poor education, that he was not able to present his case for the prize money awarded him by the British navy, so he lost that. To-day he is in our town on relief, unable to do a day's work and he is a burden on the community there. I think it is absolutely unfair that a case of this kind should receive no consideration from any of the governments concerned. In the first place I would like to ask with regard to the five per cent not being awarded this veteran.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I might answer all these matters raised by the last speakers by referring to the Pension Act. Section 5 of that act states:
Subject to the provisions of this act and of any regulations made thereunder, the commission-
That is, the Canadian pension commission:

shall have full and unrestricted power and authority and exclusive jurisdiction to deal with and adjudicate upon all matters and questions relating to the award, increase, decrease, suspension or cancellation of any pension under this act.
This would indicate that in its wisdom parliament has declared that the Canadian pension commission, within its sphere, is absolutely supreme. It never has been thought wise to give the minister or the government the right to adjudicate upon pensions or to adjust pensions. I know that in England under certain very restricted conditions the minister may award pensions. I fear that if such legislation had been in force in this country, however, the complaints which we hear now would be multiplied a hundred, yes a thousandfold.
Having regard to the twenty years in which I have been in the house, and in which I have been interested in matters concerning

Supply-Pensions and National Health
returned soldiers, may I say that if there is one department of government which has kept free from political influence and which has allowed the duly appointed judges to carry on their work without interference, it is this department. There is no possibility in any way, shape or form of influencing any of those who were appointed under the statute to carry out the duties in connection with war pensions. As a matter of fact, I have been in the department now for nearly eighteen months and I think there are at least four members of the pension commission whom I do not even know by sight. I do not know them, unless I happened to know them before I came into the department. Otherwise I have taken no steps to meet them.
The members of the appeal court are Judge Hyndman, a distinguished jurist from Alberta; Mr. Sherwood of Ottawa, and Mr. Richard of New Brunswick. Last year, as a result of the legislation and as a result of complaints made that perhaps the court did not give due attention to medical questions which arose in a great many of these cases, Doctor Kee, who had probably from fifteen to twenty years of experience as a medical officer, and later as pension commissioner, was afterwards transferred to the court of appeal, thereby becoming a member of the appeal court.
The pension commissioners, of whom one is Sir Richard Turner, usually carry out their duties two at a time, in what is called a quorum. We endeavour-and I think we nearly always succeed-to have one member of the quorum a man familiar with medicine, one who is in fact a medical practitioner. The other is a civilian, sometimes a lawyer and sometimes, as in the case of Sir Richard Turner, a man who has had a long experience in business.
Of course I cannot discuss with the hon. member for Temiscouaba the case he has in mind, or give my opinion as to whether or not in that particular case the claimant was entitled to a pension. These cases are fully considered. The evidence is taken down and is thoroughly weighed by the judges who, in these matters have as much authority as have any of the judges of the civil courts in the provinces. After they have given a decision, I am not in any way empowered, nor would I wish to have the authority to interfere.
Many people are of the opinion that all these judges should be medical men. I find that during the course of years these opinions seem to vary. At one time soldiers' organizations made representations that they did not want any lawyers or doctors to sit on any
of the courts. At another time and in another period they have said, "We want doctors" and, at another time, "We want lawyers."

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: They were right the last time.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: It depends upon the case in court, and what the decision of the quorum has been. In any event we have endeavoured to meet the wishes of all people by forming a quorum composed of one layman and one doctor.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
May I say a word to the minister and the committee regarding the appeal court, and its operation since a doctor was appointed last year. If hon. members will recall, when the matter came up before the special committee on pensions last year, the thought in the minds of members of the committee and particularly myself was that if there was a doctor on the appeal court, any doubt with respect to physical disability would be considered by a man competent to give a proper judgment. But as one who has attended the appeal court on a number of occasions, may I point out to the minister one case in which I took part only a few days ago. I shall endeavour to show that the returned man is not now getting the full advantage of having only one doctor on the appeal court. The case I have in mind is one of a man who had been too young when he enlisted; as a matter of fact, at time of enlistment he was only fourteen years of age. He had suffered an injury, but before that injury he had been taken out of the ranks and sent back as being under age. Eventually he developed a tubercular bone in the foot and at the age of thirty-six years is now incapacitated by tuberculosis.
A few days ago he appealed to the court, three judges of which were not of the medical profession. The whole case resolved itself into the question whether or not the tubercular bone might be the cause of tuberculosis for a man one hundred per cent disability. I could not help but think to myself-in fact I so stated to the judge-that it would be just as competent for me to go before the Supreme Court of Canada to argue some of the involved legal cases as it was for these three men to discuss as to whether or not the ailment was as serious as had been stated.
May I point out to the minister that a decision was rendered there and then, with no medical man present to give his views and opinion with respect to the physical disabilities of the applicant. I say to the minister and to the committee that it is high time the court of review itself was reviewed. Hope is raised in the breasts of all pensioners who
1324	COMMONS
Supply-Pensions and National Health
make application, after going through the pension commission, and from there to the quorum, that when their case comes before the appeal court there is yet some hope of a favourable decision being granted. I think the minister will agree that the percentage of cases going through the appeal court in which applicants are successful is very, very small, probably not half of one per cent. In the event of an appeal, however, the hopes of the applicant are raised, and if a decision is to be judged from or hinges on the physical disabilities of the applicant, a medical practitioner should be in attendance. I refer to the case in. which I took part a few days ago to bring to the attention of the minister the fact that the appointment of only one dioctor is not helping very much those cases which to a great extent depend upon medical evidence. If it is not thought advisable to appoint more doctors, then. I say to the minister it is high time we reviewed the appeal court.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
As one who has personally handled a great many pension cases, in view of the criticisms of the pension tribunal and the pension appeal court I feel it incumbent upon me to support the minister's statement. I would go still further. Probably because from 1928 to 1935 I represented a riding which had more people in it than had any other riding in Canada, one with an extraordinary percentage of returned soldiers, and because I have had occasion to handle a tremendous number of pension claims, my experience has been that the general administration of the act by the pension tribunal has been just and equitable, having regard to the limitations placed upon the commissioners by the statute. I have appeared before the appeal court as a lawyer only three times and the court ruled against me twice, so my opinion cannot be said to be biased by favourable results. I have had some experience in courts of law, and I want to say that I have never heard judgments more judicial and based upon sounder grounds than those delivered by the pension appeal court. When I appeared before the court, it had on it two members who are still there, Mr. Justice Hyndman and Colonel Sherwood. The other gentleman was not then a member.
I must disagree entirely with the reasoning of the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid). If he would like to have a demonstration of the considered unanimity of opinion to be got from a number of medical gentlemen, I should like to have him attend a meeting where a board of doctors is trying
(Mr. Reid.]
to decide some question of medical research with medical men appearing before the board who have different opinions.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I did not advocate a medical
board.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I do not suggest that the hon. member did, but he seemed to have an idea that the doctor appointed as medical adviser to the pension appeal court is not functioning.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
He is not the medical
adviser; be was the medical adviser, but it was thought well to appoint a doctor as a member of the appeal court. Doctor Kee is the member of the court, but as the quorum is only three, he does not sit all the time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: When he does not sit, the court have the advantage of the advice of a medical man who is removed from bias in the case. They have the advantage of his opinion in helping them to come to a judicial decision. I had a great deal of experience with Doctor Kee when he was acting in a previous capacity.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
He was chief medical
adviser to the board of pension commissioners in the old days and was afterwards appointed to the board.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I must say that I found
Doctor Kee in both capacities to be a well balanced and considerate medical man, always desirous of giving the returned soldier every possible consideration. I want hon. members to believe me when I say that I did not know Doctor Kee until I came into contact with him in connection with pension cases.
I realize there are individual cases where there would seem to be great hardship, but for every case such as those cited by the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot), by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid), and by the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), I guarantee that there are ten in which the judgments are entirely fair. From some of the utterances I have heard to-night I am inclined to think that this parliament is trying to load on to the pension board and pension appeal court a responsibility that belongs to us alone. We must face this responsibility. This parliament in its wisdom originally determined that every man who served overseas should not have a pension. Let us get that clear. This parliament said that before a man could get a pension it must be determined that the condition from which he was suffering was attributable to his military service.

Supply-Pensions and National Health

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Or incurred on.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
That was then divided into two classifications: was it because of or incurred on his military service or, in the alternative, was the condition from which he is now suffering one which existed prior to enlistment and had been aggravated by his service. We in this parliament laid down that test and the struggle of the pension commissioners and the pension appeal court has always been to ascertain that. Once that has been ascertained, the matter of assessment of disability is not nearly so difficult.
The minister has pointed out that the pension commissioners and the pension appeal court had very wide powers under section five, but he did not emphasize the fact that those powers must be exercised within the limits of the statute known as the Pension Act. That statute was passed and the limits prescribed by this parliament. As a result of laborious and painstaking inquiries by pension committees from time to time-these pension committees were in the main, if not entirely, composed of returned soldier members of this house-this parliament has in its wisdom continued the act in its present form. In every case where you find a man who cannot get a pension and who feels he is entitled to one, if you take the trouble to trace the matter down you will find that he has not been able to establish to the satisfaction of a quorum of the pension tribunal the fact that his present condition was incurred on or aggravated by his service. We prescribed that limitation, so why put the blame upon the pension tribunal or the pension appeal court? If I had any criticism to make of the administration-I want to point out that this is only my opinion and better lawyers with wider experience may disagree with me- it would be that the pension appeal court does not give sufficient weight to that section of the act which provides that a man shall have the benefit of the doubt.
In conclusion I want to join with the minister in one statement he made. I want to make it clear to every returned soldier in this country who is seeking a pension that there is not and has not been at any time any political influence or interference in connection with the work of the pension commissioners or the pension appeal court. Moreover, I have such a high opinion of the gentlemen who occupy these quasi judicial positions on the pension tribunal and the pension appeal court that I am confident they would not tolerate any such interference if it were attempted.
Mr. O'NEILL: I cannot agree with the hon. member who has just spoken (Mr. Lawson). I am more inclined to agree with the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid), the hon. member for Temiseouata (Mr. Pouliot) and the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). There is one matter I should like to mention, and that is the benefit of the doubt clause. When a man has been accepted by the army as one hundred per cent physically fit for service overseas, after he comes back from service in an active theatre of war and is discharged from the army and is not one hundred per cent physically fit, I do not think the onus should be placed on him to prove that his service overseas was the cause of his physical disability. The onus I think should be on the country to prove that that is not so. I have an outstanding case in mind. A man from British Columbia went overseas one hundred per cent physically fit. When he returned he was not physically fit, and he was discharged from the army as not physically fit. After doctoring for some' time he eventually died. From the medical records of those days it would appear that there was no doubt at all that his death was directly attributable to service overseas, but unfortunately the doctors' records were consumed in a fire before his widow could establish claim for pension. The only record available at the present time is that of the doctor who attended him in his illness, and that doctor has taken an affidavit that the man's death was directly attributable to service overseas; yet the widow of that soldier has never received a pension.
I have another case. One of the finest specimens of physical manhood that I ever saw came from Kamloops, British Columbia. He was an old countryman, a Scotchman or an Englishman; he was not a Canadian. He enlisted, and to-day that man is living in Victoria, a physical wreck. I do not think there is very much doubt that he came back from overseas a wreck directly attributable to his service overseas. He does not receive a pension sufficient to keep him and his family of three children and his wife. He gets a forty per cent pension and he has a one hundred per cent disability. The onus is placed on him to prove that his present condition is attributable to his overseas service. I think it was the present minister-and I give him credit for it-who was responsible for that clause in the act, but it seems to me to give the benefit of the doubt to the government rather than to the returned man.
Another outstanding case I might mention is that of a man now lying in King Edward sanatorium at Kamloops, who may never be
1326	COMMONS
Supply-Pensions and National Health
discharged from that sanatorium as cured. He has been in it almost ever since he got out of the navy. About six months after he was discharged from the navy his case was diagnosed as tuberculosis. Since that man when he enlisted was accepted as one hundred per cent physically fit, and since he has served the empire in the day of need, I think that whether his present condition is directly attributable to his service overseas or not, we should try to pay our debt to him. He served us when we needed him, and we ought to serve him now that he needs us. We have plenty of money for defence purposes, plenty of money for anything and everything except for the returned men, and if there is one class of men in this country who are now entitled to something it is the returned men. That is the point I want to make, Mr. Chairman. is,	there is the law, and the pension tribunal and the appeal court are bound to enforce
it.	All I have to say is, let us be fair and honest about the thing. Do not let us be criticizing the administration unless it becomes a question of administration. their disability, but no administration and no law can bring perfect and equal justice to all people. I think the administration of our pension legislation brings a measure of justice equal to that of our courts of justice, which function in respect of property and civil rights

speechtext: If I might be permitted one minute to reply, if the hon. gentleman sat here till doomsday he would never know as much law as I do, but as the length of his service in this parliament increases he will find that it is the part of wisdom and good judgment in pension matters to pay some heed to the recommendation of a parliamentary committee, itself consisting of returned men, which has spent hours and days investigating the problem and comes back to this house with a recommendation.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I do not think there are any members in this house, and there are very few people throughout the country, who do not wish to see the returned soldier treated fairly and squarely by this government and by the people of Canada. In my experience as a medical man I have seen throughout the dominion returned men who I believe are deserving of pension and who are not receiving it. On the other hand, I agree with the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lawson) that there are very, very many returned soldiers who are to-day receiving more pension than they deserve. They are receiving the benefit of the doubt. The doctors are trying to treat the returned soldiers fairly. They are giving them the benefit of the doubt, and many returned soliders, I repeat, are receiving more pension than they absolutely deserve.
But there is one thing, Mr. Chairman, that is troubling not only the returned soldier but the private citizen in this country. There are a great many returned men who have been wounded and are now receiving a pension of seventy-five or a hundred per cent, and at the same time they are working for the government and getting one hundred per cent salary. People cannot understand how

Sup-ply-Pensions and National Health
a man can be one hundred per cent disabled and yet be one hundred per cent efficient; it is absolutely impossible. We know men who at present are drawing one hundred per cent salaries, running from eight to nine thousand dollars a year, and at the same time drawing one hundred per cent pensions running from two to three thousand dollars. One or the other is wrong. When a man is receiving a one hundred per cent salary, if he is getting from seventy-five to one hundred per cent pension his pension should be stopped until he is no longer able to do his work, and then his pension should start again. This is something that is worrying the returned soldiers, because many of them to-day are on relief, and they believe that these other men are in their way, taking positions that they could fill. Either of these things should stop. The minister should investigate the matter, and I urge him to consider the possibility of rectifying what I regard as an evil.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Of all those who have
spoken to-night I am inclined to agree more with the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. O'Neill) than with anyone else. As a member of this house I accept the challenge of my good friend the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lawson), that the government should introduce legislation to give justice to the man who went overseas and fought our battles. If they will introduce such legislation I will support them.
The hon. member for Kamloops says that the fact that a man offered his services when the country was in dire need should be sufficient to entitle him to proper consideration and a decent livelihood for the rest of his life, and I agree with that. I have submitted to the minister the complaints and requests of a number of returned soldiers; I have also gone to the pension board, and I must say that in all cases the members of the board have shown me the utmost courtesy.
I believe the board has been serious in its desire to rectify any wrong that has been done these men, but there is one particular case I want to bring to the attention of the minister to-night. I am referring now to a soldier who to-day is only forty-two years of age and who enlisted as a very young man. I believe he was discharged as physically fit; at any rate he did not ask for a pension until six or seven years ago when he began to feel the effects of his war service and requested a medical examination. After six years of medical examinations, during which time he has appeared before different boards, they have now reached the stage where they 31111-84
admit that they cannot do anything for him, notwithstanding that he had a wonderful record of service overseas. He was wounded three or four times; he was gassed; he had tonsilitis and a broken ankle and was buried by a shell and extricated by two of his comrades. The authorities have been impressed by his war service; yet they find they cannot do anything for him as far as a pension is concerned.
This man wrote to me two weeks ago and I was struck with his case as one that deserves the most serious consideration the minister can possibly give it. I asked this man whether he would allow me to submit his letter to the House of Commons and he said, "use it in any way you see fit." I wish to read this letter because it shows how bitter some of these men are becoming at the way in which they have been used. I believe this is an isolated case, because on the whole the returned men have been used very well; but there are cases such as this that should have the attention of the minister. The letter reads:
Dear Sir:
I am writing in regard my claim for pension. I am sure there is a mistake about that quorum in April 1936. I was told at that quorum that they granted in my favour. I was also notified to that effect, but they sent it to Montreal for hearing. I do not know what for and neither do they unless it was to do me out of it, so I think they have told you wrong. Such stuff to tell anyone, they don't think my disability came from service. ' I just wish the fool that said no had the ailments I have, they would belly ache. I suppose wounded, gassed and the rest done me a lot of real good instead of injuring me and my health leave out long service in trenches in mud and water to my waist for this country only to have dirt handed me always. Sir, if I had not of got clothing this winter from two different parties in the city I do not know how my children would of got to school and still they are short of sweaters and bed clothes a great country and fairness Eh? I don't think: I am sending you a copy of my old tribunal case that was held at Winnipeg, read it and then you will know why I am just plain mad and bitter. Please see if you can find out why they went against that, enough for any man to get a pension on. Will you please return that paper to me, I want to keep it. I am appealing but what good will it do. I am sending forms to Mr. Masterman, would you please see that they bring my case up and not hold it six more years if I get a pension or not. I am told that an appeal is supposed to be taken up at once.
I forgot to state that any doubt in the case was supposed to be given in my favour, is it? Same old thing, is the like of this to be allowed?
The hon. member for Wood Mountain (Mr. Donnelly) said that some of these returned men had been retired on pensions of one hundred or seventy-five per cent and were now

1328	COMMONS
Supply-Pensions and National Health
in good positions enjoying reasonable salaries. Well, perhaps that could be objected to on reasonable grounds. But what about C. P. Fullerton, who, after serving the country for twenty years and receiving $250,000 from the taxpayers, has been granted a pension of $6,000 as an ex-judge? And he is not helpless; he has no disability that we know of. I say this because he has now started business in Toronto and will probably earn $30,000 or $40,000 a year in his law practice. There is no justice in this. The awarding of pensions in Canada is anything but equitable. However, this is by the way. What I am particularly concerned with at the moment is to make a plea for this man whose case I have brought to the attention of the minister, and I trust the minister will give it his most serious consideration.

speechtext: I do not think there is any use in bringing up particular cases. I believe it can be said that every man in this house, no matter to which party he belongs, is behind the minister and wishes to see the returned man get a square deal. The minister is a big-hearted fellow; I have known him a good many years and I trust him. I have never yet seen a minister who did not Want to give the returned man a square deal, and I think it is bad advertising to talk as we are doing in this house.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I do not know that I agree with a great deal that has been said this evening. I wonder Whether we are sincerely behind'the minister to see that the returned soldier gets a square deal. maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: What about the last one?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
