speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I do not think I can let that go by. It was easy to let everyone have their word to say about the poor unfortunate commission and the appeal court, but may I say that, in my opinion, although there was only one member of the court with whose appointment I had anything to do, I believe the court is carrying on its duty as well as it can under the circumstances. As the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lawson) has

said, it is interpreting the law placed on our statute books by the different parliaments of Canada which have succeeded one another since the war. This legislation is the result of the efforts of no one government and no one political party; this Pension Act, revised, amended, modified and changed, as it now stands, has been so modified on the recommendation of one parliamentary committee after another sitting almost every year since 1916. I suppose I am now the only member of this house who has been on every such committee since 1918, when I first came into the house. I should like to tell my hon. friend who is new to this house that in those committees there never was the least suspicion of any party politics-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I never said there was.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Time after time these committees came before the House of Commons and the house decided that it was in the best interests of the soldiers and of the country to accept, I think in almost every case unanimously, the reports of those committees. That happened last year; it happened in 1933, 1930, 1928, 1924, 1922, 1921, 1920, 1919, 1918, 1917 and 1916. In no instance within my recollection has there been any partisan discussion of the reports of those committees. Yet my hon. friend says that this government, like every government since the war, is chiselling on the returned soldier. I have heard that accusation made many times. We are discussing pensions now; the returned soldier who asks for a pension should at least show that the disability from which he is suffering was incurred during or was due to his military service. There is no association-there has not been prior to recent months at least- no organization of any standing in the community, looking after returned men which has ever suggested that pensions should be given on the basis of service alone. It has been an accepted principle that for a man to obtain war pension from this country he must show, first, that he is disabled and, second, that his disability is in some measure due to or was incurred during service. In 1930, when I was chairman of the pension committee, there was inserted in the act a clause which provided that in cases of this kind the applicant should be given the benefit of reasonable doubt. I do not propose to discuss here the question whether or not the judges appointed under the authority of this parliament do in every case give the benefit of the doubt. But I will say that it must be extremely difficult for any award of pension to be made at this late date unless there is a great deal of benefit of the doubt given.

Supply-Pensions and National Health
There has been some discussion of the pension quorums and of the appeal court. Let me put this to the committee : When a pension application is first made, it goes to the Canadian pension commission. Without seeing the soldier, because the Canadian pension commission's head office is here in Ottawa, they examine the case on the basis of the documents on the file. A decision is arrived at as to whether or not the pension shall be awarded. The figures given last year before the committee indicated that at first hearing something like 30 per cent of the applications were granted;-and; it is now, mind you, twenty years after the
war.	so that without some benefit of the doubt being given it must be extremely difficult for the applicant to make any case. If the application is refused! by the Canadian pension commission, it can go before a quorum of the commission, which, as hon. members know, sits as nearly as possible in the locality where the applicant resides, sees the applicant, hears his case presented through a veterans' bureau by advocates appointed by the government, and there again it is decided whether or not he is entitled to pension. In this court the percentage of claims granted last year,
was,	I think, 15 per cent; I speak subject to correction; it may have run to 18 per cent. If the applicant is turned down there in the second instance, he has the right to go to the appeal court. Naturally, before the appeal court is reached the good cases are nearly all sifted out; nearly every one who has any chance of obtaining pension has been eliminated before the appeal court is reached. Nevertheless this country, which my hon. friend accuses of chiselling the soldier, pays his lawyer, pays the doctors to look after him, sets up all this expensive machinery and gives him the right to apply to the appeal court for nothing, and because the man knows it will cost him nothing, it is a sweepstake so far as he is concerned; he might just as well go to appeal because he has a possible chance of getting his pension and it costs him nothing to try. The whole machinery is paid for by the country. He goes to the appeal court, and I think it is only reasonable to suppose that that court could not in the ordinary course be expected to grant pension in such a high percentage of cases as is the case in the lower courts. So what may be meant by chiselling on the soldier I do not know.
We cannot give pensions to everybody; at least no one has ever asked that we give pensions to everyone. We cannot give treatment to everyone. A great many of the returned soldiers who are at present suffering 31111-844
from disabilities have now reached an age, forty-nine, fifty, sixty, when normally in civilian life their health is not as good as when they were twenty-five, and naturally they may think it is due to their war service. But it is very difficult to assess the degree, if any,, to which the disability from which they are suffering is due to their wrar service. For that reason a large number of them do not get pension. But I do not think it shows that the governments have been chiselling on the returned soldier when upwards of one billion dollars have been paid out to returned soldiers since the war, a sum equivalent to the whole amount collected in income tax from the people of Canada since income tax was instituted, and when we are paying an annual bill running from $41,000,000 to $45,000,000.
Before I close I should like to make this further point. I have said to my department; I have said outside; I have said at gatherings of soldiers and elsewhere, that it matters not one whit to me if the pension bill amounts to $45,000,000, to $50,000,000 or more. What I am interested in is seeing to it that every soldier who is entitled to a pension under the legislation which parliament has enacted shall get it and, as far as it lies within my power, I am making every possible effort to see that this is done. I am not trying to economize in pensions. I should not mind if the pension bill were very much higher, but I am opposed, in the interests of the soldiers as much as in the interests of the country, to any general distribution of funds for service only.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I do not want the committee or 1he Minister of Pensions and National Health to think I am offering any criticism of the administration of his department by himself or by his predecessors since the great war. I have listened to the remarks of some hon. gentlemen in this committee, and I do feel that the trouble with the Pension Act is that it is not sufficiently elastic; that there is no discretionary power vested in any person to take into consideration the rights of the individual in any particular case and to treat that case as it should be treated.
In my constituency in the city of Halifax I have two particular cases which I am going to bring to the attention of the minister and hon. members of this house. One case, Mr. Chairman, is that of a nurse who went overseas. She might have gone over on the Llandovery Castle; to-day she might have been in the watery deep. I would call your attention, sir, to the fact that it is impossible to make remarks in this house while conversations are going on to such an exteht as to interfere with continuity of thought. That
1330	COMMONS
Supply-Pensions and National Health
remark has reference not to the minister but rather to those who perhaps do not realize that they are interfering with the proceedings .of this committee.
This nurse reached the age of sixty-five a tew months ago. If she had served for another year and two months she would have been entitled to a pension. Now, however, she has been cast out into the streets without one dollar, without a home, without any person to protect her, and under the act there seems to be no provision under which her case might be given consideration or under which her time might be built up by service. Those in authority at Camp Hill hospital at Halifax say she is still competent as a nurse but that she must retire, and notwithstanding her splendid services overseas and at the hospital since the war she is left without a pension. She is practically on the poor list in the city of Halifax. That, Mr. Chairman, is a case where there should be elasticity; there should be some discretionary power vested either in the minister or in some board so that this nurse might be cared for and put on a basis whereby for the rest of her years- which may be only five or ten-at least she might receive some recognition of her services to her country, particularly as a woman.
The other case is that of a man of about thirty-five years of age, living in the city of Halifax. From this family four brothers went overseas. Three of them are dead. This chap of whom I speak was gassed and] wounded twice. He went into his last battle and was shot in the head. Now he receives the magnificent pension of $7.50 per month, and from the city of Halifax he receives $10 a month. That is a total of $17.50, all of which he has to pay for his room and board. He has very severe pains in his chest and some kind friends sent him to an outstanding specialist-, and now he has found that his patient has developed tuberculosis. So to-day in the city of Halifax he is receiving $7.50 plus $10 per month, and he has no recourse. There is no elasticity in the act; he has no opportunity to have his case reviewed.
In my judgment, Mr. Chairman, I believe some provision should be made for cases of this kind. I do not believe there is anyone more sympathetic to the returned men than the present Minister of Pensions and National Health, who is also a returned man. One has had to be there to know and understand what men go through, both physically and mentally, in the awful battles that take place in any war such as that which lasted from 1914 to 1918. Sometimes committees of this house bring in reports, but they do not get down to the practical thought that while
[Mr. Filin.j
a case may be made out, while a man may have a bona fide claim and may be honest, sincere and deserving, it may not come within the four corners of the act as it exists to-day, and that the act should be so amended as to permit of cases of this kind being looked after, so that the returned man who has gone through what this chap went through may be cared for. This man of whom I speak is the last of four brothers. They all went overseas, and as a matter of fact his father served in the South African war. This man to whom I refer is now receiving $17.50 per month, though he is suffering with his head and from tuberculosis. It appears to me that this is a travesty on the act, and I say it is up to the parliament of this country, in which I have the honour to have a seat, to remedy cases of this kind by the necessary amendments to the act in order to give the technical officers of the department the right to deal with such cases. I suggest that they should be handled in this way, submitted for the consideration of the government or the appeal board, and then dealt with by order in council.
I had the privilege of attending before the appeal court in Ottawa, presided over by Judge Hyndman. I want to say that that court is as human and as ready and willing to go as far as possible as any court could be. When the case before it had been presented by Mr. Hogan, the returned soldiers' advocate Judge Hyndman turned to me and said, "Mr. Finn, do you desire to say anything to the court?" I said, "No. I came here because I believe this is a worthy case." He said, "I only wish there was a greater interest shown by members in their constituencies. I wish they would come and give that moral support which sometimes is so necessary to those who feel they have not received justice." In that particular case the decision was that the returned man was entitled to a substantial pension. The war ended in 1918 and this case was last year, and it is only a matter of addition to know the number of years which have passed since then -nineteen years. During all that time he was not in receipt of a pension which the appeal court, the final tribunal, awarded him in a judgment handed down.
I offer these suggestions to the Minister of Pensions and National Health and to hon. members of the committee, and at the same time suggest there should be an amendment to the act whereby in equitable cases the minister might have the case presented to him, in consultation with the appeal court. Finally, a recommendation might be made to the governor in council so that specially

Sup-ply-Pensions and National Health
deserving cases which have been unfairly considered-not intentionally, but by reason of the narrow scope of the act-might be given further favourable consideration.
I have given two concrete examples in order to show the necessity for elasticity. That can be brought about only by an amendment whereby discretion would be given to some person so that a returned soldier might have an opportunity of a rehearing and final decision. The two examples I have given are sufficient for me, as a member of the legal profession, and are outside any sympathetic interest I may have in returned soldiers. I had the misfortune of losing a young nephew, Lieutenant Clifford Finn, who served overseas. Just before the armistice three machine gun bullets passed through the back of his neck and at the age of eighteen years he was killed. The colonel of his regiment wrote saying that his last words were, "Get the boys under cover. I am going out." I asked my late brother, Doctor W. D. Finn, how it was possible the boy could speak, three bullets having gone through the back of his neck, and his reply was, "Well, Bob, that is possible. The spinal column was cut off, but for a few seconds the clarity of the brain was so great that it gave him an opportunity to think of others." At that moment he, himself, was ready to drop, and never again did he breathe the breath of life.
I want to pay tribute at this time to the hon. member for Argenteuil (Sir George Per-ley), and to thank him for the sincerity and the splendid sympathy he showed to all men who served overseas. He was the representative of Canada, looking after the interests of those men who were fighting the cause of democracy. I believe I would not be out of order in saying that I wondered if whether democracy had failed when last night, after going to bed, I read that the son-in-law of Haile Selassie had been shot within an hour after he had been captured, by order of Mussolini.

speechtext:
I promise the hon. member
for Kamloops (Mr. O'Neill) one hundred per cent support, if he proposes to do something worth while for the returned soldier. In the past, when we needed cannon fodder, our men have been provided for. We have given them uniforms; we have given them $1.10 a day, and we have made millionaires out of our munitions makers. I believe the Minister of Pensions (Mr. Power) said that since that time we have paid one billion dollars in payment of war pensions and in addition we have paid millions of dollars in interest on war debts. Yet to-day we have thousands of our returned men on the breadline, or very close to it. What are we doing to help them? We are spending a good deal of time balking, but what action are we taking? It is about time we realized our responsibilities. If I wished to take the time of the committee I could, describe cases which have been brought to my attention, but on this occasion I shall' not do so.
I do not wish to criticize the minister, nor do I criticize the commission looking after this part of the work. If their efforts are within the law, that is all they can do. But as members of the House of Commons and as representatives of the people, including large numbers of returned soldiers, it is our duty to do something worth while, and to do "it at this session. Our returned soldiers have suffered long enough; let us now help them a little bit.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I do not wish unduly to detain the committee, but may I say that I agree with the hon. member who has just spoken.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, parliament has been most earnest in its desire to bring pension legislation to the greatest point of efficiency. The minister has spoken about the advantages received by ex-service men through an advocate. I now appeal to him to give a resident advocate to the interior of British Columbia. When one was originally appointed, his seat of activities was supposed to be at Nelson, but his duties at Vancouver have become so onerous that he seldom reaches the interior. Four-fifths of the exservice men of British Columbia are located

Supply-Pensions and National Health
at the coast, a factor which works distinctly ito the disadvantage of the men in the interior as they do not have an opportunity to bring their complaints to his attention.
Something has been said about ex-service men discharged as physically fit. We know that when the war closed the great desire of the men was to get home. Sometimes they were discharged as physically fit, after only very short examinations. These are the men who to-day have the greatest difficulty in appealing for pensions. When quorums visit a community, applicants appear in person, and the members of those quorums are able to judge as to a man's physical condition. When the man's condition is supported by the word of a local physician, it seems unreasonable that an appeal court should take a view contrary to that expressed by the quorum. My observations are particularly applicable when the local physician is acting under the instructions of the department.
In this connection I urge, first of all, that the minister give thought to placing an advocate in the interior and, second, that the decision of the quorum be final without opportunity on the part of the government to appeal. I have appeared before the board of pension commissioners in a great many cases and my experience has been that they give a most sympathetic hearing to the cases which come before them. This is particularly so of Judge Taylor and General McDonald. I simply want to urge again that the minister give thought to appointing a soldiers' advocate in the interior of the province.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I shall be very glad to look into the question of the appointment of an advocate in the interior of British Columbia. I believe Mr. Markham was at Nelson but was transferred to Vancouver. Because of the great amount of work at Vancouver, two advocates are located there. Mr. Drinnan and Mr. Markham are located at Vancouver and Mr. Sedger is located at Victoria.
In connection with appeals to the pension appeal court, I am assuming that the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Esling) is referring to appeals by the crown. From 193132 to May, 1933, there were 2,947 appeals taken by commission counsel, that is by the crown. On many of those appeals the decision of the old tribunals was reversed. Since 1933 there have been only 152 appeals by the crown, so surely it cannot be said that the crown has abused its power of appeal since that time. The ratio is 152 in approximately three years as compared with 2,947 in two years.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the
minister has referred to section five as conferring wide powers upon the appeal court. I can understand that this court should have wide powers and be free from political interference, but I cannot understand why they should be empowered to brush aside what would appear to be well known British legal procedure and jurisprudence. As I understood the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lawson), when a man has established his claim before a commission quorum he is reasonably assured of his pension, but many appeals from the quorum tribunals are reversed by the appeal court. I know that many men in my constituency have established their cases before the quorum tribunal, but when the government appealed to the appeal court, which did not have the advantage of hearing the witnesses- a procedure which to my mind is contrary to every rule of British jurisprudence-the appeal was allowed.
I know of one man who was in the trenches for three and a half years. He did not receive a scratch, but he is one of those burnt-out cases. He is a physical wreck and is absolutely unable to earn his own living. As you know, we have no relief in New Brunswick at the present time and the condition of this man and his family is absolutely pitiful. His claim was allowed by a quorum of the commission but it was disallowed by the appeal court. It seems to me that something should be done for cases like this. The minister has stated that where cases have been disallowed by the quorum, an appeal could be taken to the appeal court. But in this case the claim was allowed by the quorum and appealed by the government. I think the law should be changed as it is hard to convince the man on the street that it is being fairly administered. This is especially so, when they see men who are apparently in the pink of condition getting large pensions.
I know of other similar cases but I shall not cite them this evening. I know of cases where men were received into the army as physically fit, and yet were demobilized for medical unfitness. Surely if they were fit when they went into the army and unfit when they came out, their unfitness must be due to their service. If the doctors made a mistake in the first place, then the government should be estopped from claiming that the man's disabilities dated back prior to enlistment. If the doctors had not their eyes open and did not do their work properly, I think the government should suffer the consequences.

Supply-Pensions and National Health

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I do not want to be misunderstood. I was casting absolutely no reflection on the officials of the department. I believe the officials of this department are among the most efficient in the government service. I did not infer that there had ever been any political partisanship displayed.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
My hon. friend, says that there are seventy or eighty lawyers in this house, and suggests that they might draft the necessary legislation to meet these cases. I am sure he does not desire that statement to go out to the country because, while I happen to belong to the legal profession and know the rules which govern parliament and the expenditure of public moneys, and while I might be competent with the other legal members of the house to draft an amendment to meet these extreme cases which have been mentioned here to-night, the fact remains that no member of this house, outside the members of the government, can. introduce a bill and get it
to its second, reading if it involves the expenditure of public money. Such a bill must emanate from a member of the cabinet sitting on the treasury benches or meet with their approval.
My hon. friend spoke of the law of estoppel. It is perhaps one of the most intricate pieces of law to interpret and establish that come before our courts. While a person may 'be estopped, in the pension law as it stands upon the statute books to-day there is no provision dealing with the law of estoppel. That question can only be pleaded to courts of law. I do think, however, Mr. Chairman, that when a serious submission is made to the Minister of Pensions and to the government for an amendment that would make the law more elastic in order to deal with these cases, our efforts should not cease with the member who urges such an amendment trying to make himself au fait with his constituents-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
My hon. friend says, "Hear,
hear," and I say, "There, there." When I suggest a thing in this house, it is not to gain votes. I have had too many of them; otherwise I would not be here again. When I speak in this house I do so in order that action shall be taken and a remedy applied, and that the word "gratitude," so plain in the English language and yet so forgotten to-day, should again appear, not in a statute or an amendment, but in our dealing with the human equation. I would ask the minister if he would not consider with his colleagues the question of an amendment to the act in order to give it that elasticity of which I have spoken to-night, so that these very deserving cases, based upon truth and honesty and right, shall have an opportunity of a rehearing, and then we may hope that the applicants may spend the remainder of their days not in poverty but with perhaps a sufficient amount that they can look forward to the next day and feel they were not like the man President Roosevelt described as the "forgotten man." In that very description of his was the reason for his great victory of four years ago, and for his practical annihiliation of all parties in the United States last November,. when, only two states, and those the ones nearest to us, voted against him. I am not talking to get votes; I am not talking to hear myself talk. I am trying to draw the attention of the Minister of Pensions and of the government to these cases. I see the Minister of Justice in. his seat. No more human man, no wiser legislator, no better draftsman, no man of keener intellect then he sits in this house, and I would appeal to him and to the

I should like to ask the
Minister of Pensions a question^ based upon a communication which I have in my hand, and which does seem -to me to present a very interesting question. It does not involve any large sum of money, nor does it involve any radical change of policy. I think the letter is worth reading:
I am a returned man, nearly stone deaf through war disability. There is a bone conduction aceousticon on the market that enables me to hear nearly as good as before I got this head injury. Christie hospital authorities have been trying to get one for me for a long time, but the Ottawa authorities state there is no money available to purchase these things with.
I got a loan of one of these instruments once, and with it I heard my first talkie. My children's voices were a revelation to me, and they v'ere tickled to think they could talk to me without raising the roof or letting the people in the next town hear what they had to say to me.	.
The government supplies artificial limbs tor amputation cases; why not aids to hearing! The retail price is $100, but I am unable to o that high. I am a widower with four ealthy youngsters to feed, and being a one hundred per cent disability case I can't earn anything towards the purchase of this machine. Life would start all over for me if the government gave me one.
Then he gives his name and pension number. It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that the man who writes that letter presents a very interesting point. After all, if a man has lost his arm or his leg, he is supplied with an artificial arm or leg, or if he loses an eye, he is given something to replace the eye for appearance's sake. But if a man is deaf, and cannot procure something with which to hear, he cannot hear at all. In this particular case the man is not able to buy this instrument because the cost of the acousticon is too high. I know from my personal experience with friends and relatives that the acousticon is efficient in many cases of deafness. Accordingly I would ask the minister if there is not some provision for such a case as this, and when I ask him that question I realize that this will not open many such cases.

The War Veterans' Allowance Act provides for allowances to ex-members of the Canadian forces and to ex-members of the allied forces who were domiciled in Canada at the time of their enlistment and who served in a theatre of actual war, or, not having so served, are in receipt of a pension or have commuted a pension by final payment. The allowance is payable to such veterans upon attaining the age of sixty years or, not having attained this age, who are in the opinion of the board permanently unemployable by reason of mental or physical disability. The maximum allowance is $40 per month if the man is married or a widower with dependent children, or $20 if he is unmarried. The allowance may be continued to a widow for a period of one year.
I think it is well known to the committee that the War Veterans' Allowance Act will continue to rise in cost; the operation will be more expensive as the years go on and more and more men reach the age of sixty or become permanently incapable of carrying on their occupation.
Under the amendments of last year another class was admitted to allowances. I have already stated that the allowances provided for carrying out this act, beginning in 1930 with something like $300,000 have now risen to $4,200,000 and will rise to $12,000,000 or $13,000,000 a year.

The government sent a number of geologists throughout the country to try to find mines, but having found them they said, in effect, " Now, go to it and see what you can do." I think there should be some branch of the department to follow up these matters further. In this case apparently it is a question of roads, and I should iiice to

see the department take whatever means may be available in order to induce the appropriate authority having charge of the construction of roads to get busy and see that the road is kept open so that the operation of the mine will not be interfered with. I should like to hear from the minister as to the prospects of the chromium mine of Collins, Ontario, becoming more completely developed for the benefit of the steel industry of Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. T. A. CRERAR (Minister of Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: This chromium mine, which, as my hon. friend has stated, is located in the Port Arthur district is, as I recall it, some eighteen or twenty miles from the National Transcontinental railway. The ore is taken to the railway by motor transport and then shipped to Sault Ste. Marie, where it is smelted. Some assistance was given in the building or improvement of the road from the mine to the railway last summer.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: By this department?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Yes, out of the vote passed a year ago for aid to roads to mining areas. I am afraid I have not information as to the actual amount of money spent last year in this connection, but I would say for the information of the hon. member that expenditures were made in cooperation with the provinces. The federal Department of Mines put up two dollars for each dollar advanced by the provinces.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Does the minister mean two dollars a ton?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: No, not two dollars a ton. For each two dollars we put up, the province puts up one dollar for the improvements of the roads. The projects were agreed upon after consultation between the mines branch at Ottawa and the mines departments in each of the provinces. The latest information I have is that progress is being made by the company and that they are enlarging not only the capacity of their mine, so far as the production of ore is concerned, but also the capacity of the smelter at Sault Ste. Marie.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Does one company operate both mine and smelter?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
My information is that there is a great opportunity there at the present time. The Ford Motor Company, I am told, are considering taking the full output of the mine, which would involve the full output of the smelter at Sault Ste. Marie. However, the steel company at Sault Ste. Marie can utilize a quantity of the material, and anything that can be done to increase

Supply-Mines and Resources
the production of chromium in the area would be a great benefit not only to employment at that point but also to the motor industry in Canada. The plant at Sault Ste. Marie is not small; in fact it is very substantial. I talked with the heads of the company, and they struck me as being men who understood their business. Any assistance the department could give would be of great advantage to the country and an evidence of good work by the Department of Mines.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I agree with the observations of the hon. member. I find that last year $20,000 was spent on the road from the mine to the railway. As I said a minute ago, two-thirds of that amount was put up by the federal Department of Mines, and one-third by the provincial governments. May I say for the information of the committee that this development was commenced only a few years ago. From information we have there can be no doubt that there is a very considerable body of chrome ore in the area, and the value of chromium as a medium for the hardening of steel is recognized everywhere. I have not had an opportunity recently of talking to people engaged in the enterprise, but about a year ago I did have an interview with them. They called to see me in Ottawa and they were optimistic at that time as to the future prospects of their development, and asked for some assistance in fixing up their road. That assistance was given to them. So far as I am able to learn, they are expanding their operations.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I believe it was either July or early August that I was there. Was the road fixed after that, because at that time I was informed it was not in good condition?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Yes, it was after that. As the hon. member will recall, last year we did not get the estimate through until about the end of June, and arrangements had to be made after that. I should think it would have been August or September when the expenditure was made.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Does the department know if the process in use at Sault Ste. Marie is giving all the satisfaction that was hoped?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: So far as we are aware, they are operating successfully and have developed a process which is working out successfully.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I thank the minister for his information.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
As a result of the treatment of coal in the last thirty years, in a
great many of our Canadian fuels we have about one-half of one per cent sulphur content. So far as I can remember, the method of removing the sulphur has never been improved upon. When I was a boy the coal was washed, and as much as possible of the sulphur was taken out of it. However, there was always a trace left. Would the minister consider allocating to the fuel board an amount of money sufficient to ascertain whether, by combinations or by chemical affinity, the last trace of sulphur could not be neutralized. I have made diligent inquiry, and I have been unable to find where any effort has been made to improve upon the old washing method. I am not speaking critically, and am only offering suggestions, but it is my belief that after we have had a research department for a number of years, and after we have expended so much money, the time has arrived when the people of Canada are entitled to have definite research work carried out. I make these observations only as suggestions. Perhaps by the coal being treated with hydrogen, the sulphur could be made to combine with the other elements, and in that way the difficulty might be removed. It is incumbent upon the research department of the fuel board to take the matter into consideration, in an effort to give coal absolutely free of sulphur to the people of Canada. At the present time the sulphur content is only a small fraction, but even that amount has a deleterious effect.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: The point raised by the hon. member is an important one. However, I think he is under a misapprehension when he says nothing has been done. I am informed that tests are being carried on at the fuel testing laboratory which operates in conjunction with the mines and geology branch of the department. The hon. member has referred to a matter of research. I may inform him, however, that experimental work is being carried on, and the matter to which he drew attention is being studied. Of necessity we must operate the Laboratory within the limits of the vote given by parliament, but I can assure him the work is being carried on.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Has any progress been made?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I am informed progress has been made. Apparently there are two classes of sulphur

and I must confess I am not altogether familiar with the subject. Perhaps the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie could give a better answer. I may say, however, that there are minerals containing sulphides, and on the other hand there are organic sulphurs. Experiments have been
Supply-Mines and Resources

carried on with greater success with the first than with the second kind. The difficulties to which the hon. member has referred are found in the latter, namely the organic sulphurs in coal. However, we are doing our best to eliminate the difficulty.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Is the fuel testing department supplied with money sufficient to enable it to go on with the experiments? If there is a lack of money, then I say a sufficient amount should be set aside to permit it to proceed with the work. A satisfactory solution of the difficulty would be worth millions of dollars to Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I should not want the hon. member to get the impression that there is a shortage of funds in this connection. The matter is really a research problem and I have no doubt that some day the scientists will discover a method whereby that substance can be taken from the coal.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Near Campbell's Cross, which is in my riding, is a bromine well which has attracted considerable attention. We have been informed that this is perhaps the only well capable of producing bromine in a particular chemical state. Could the minister advise whether or not there are other wells in eastern Canada with a sufficient commercial productive capacity to compete with this one?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I am afraid I cannot answer fully the question directed to me by my hon. friend. I believe he could get the information he desires by inquiring of the technical officers in the mines branch. I was unaware that there was a well of that type in his favoured district and I am at a loss to state at the moment whether there are other wells of a similar kind in eastern Canada. My deputy tells me that he is not aware of any. I shall be glad to get this information for my hon. friend or he can inquire of the technical officers who, I think, can satisfy him.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I understand this is the only bromine producer in the eastern part of Canada and I thought t'he minister would have soime information. I shall be very glad to inquire of the officials of the branch.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: As far as our information goes, that is the only well in eastern Canada.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Could the minister give us the location and the equipment of the different research laboratories connected with this department?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
There is only one associated with the mines branch, the one located on

Booth street. Experimental work is carried on in connection with the properties of coal and also in connection with the metallurgical processes best adapated to the treatment of certain ores. This laboratory has done excellent and useful work. Last summer I had an opportunity of visiting a number of large mines in Canada and I was given the voluntary information by different mine managers that the service rendered by this department for many years past had been most valuable.
I do not know whether I mentioned this a year ago, but it is worth repeating; when the representatives from the empire countries were in Ottawa in 1932 to attend the imperial conference, the Premier of Rhodesia visited the laboratory here. They had had trouble in working out a treatment for a certain kind of ore and he arranged to ship several tons here to the mines branch. The technical officers were successful in working out the correct treatment for this ore and as a result of that this mine in Rhodesia has been put into operation. This is a striking illustration of the value of the work being done in these laboratories.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: A few days ago I referred to the development of the iron mines at Helen mountain in Algoma. Since that time the Ontario government has voted a subsidy of two cents per unit for the development of this mine. The minister referred a moment ago to the assistance being given to the chromium mine at Collins whereby this government was to pay two-thirds of t)he cost of a road.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Yes, by arrangement with the provincial government.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I was wondering whether the same kind of arrangement could not be made in connection with these iron ore mines at Helen mountain. I believe this vote gives a great return to the country and perhaps the minister could give some aid by way of road assistance, to the development of this mine.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Any request to that effect would certainly receive careful consideration, but I would not want to commit myself or the government in connection with bounties, to which the hon. member referred the other night.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Is this research laboratory at the service of companies and individuals interested in mining?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
That is correct.

Questions

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Could the minister give details of this vote and how the increase is accounted for?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: The appropriation of the division of mineral resources is $22,000; for the division of ore dressing and metallurgy, $77,000. This is really the important division in this vote. Then there is $46,000 for fuels and fuel testings and $20,000 for ceramics and road materials. This is to cover a study of road materials, binding materials and so on. There is $5,000 for the chemical division and $43,000 for the mechanical section. There is $41,000 for general administration, printing, the purchase of books and contingencies, and $19,000 for expenses of the dominion fuel board?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Which item is increased over last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: The increase of $26,700 is due to some reclassifications which have been made, statutory increases and promotions.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Not the whole of it?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
It is due to promotions,
reclassifications, statutory increases and a few new positions created in extending the service.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Is there any revenue to
Canada from any of this?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
The revenue does not
amount to a great deal. There is some revenue from assays and from the sale of publications. As a matter of fact, I have under consideration at the present time making a charge for services in connection with ore-dressing processes. If a man comes in with an ore that he has had difficulty in working out a process for, and we take that in hand and work out a process for it, I think a charge could quite legitimately be made for that service. That is under consideration now.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
The reason I asked is
that the matter has been discussed for some time.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Progress reported.
On motion of Mr. Lapointe (Quebec East) the house adjourned at 10.55 p.m.
